exclusions.A: In October Merrin wrote again: the oak beams that carried the roof were sound, but the bare laths between them would collapse under a heavy snow.
exclusions.B: The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams.
exclusions.C: On the night of 9 January 1932, under eight inches of snow, the roof collapsed into the hall.
exclusions.E: In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

WV7-P01.4.note: Beams that 'carried the roof' are the structural members bearing its weight, i.e. holding it up; the other senses (moving, printing, stocking goods, hauling) do not fit a stationary roof.

exclusions.B: The council could agree on nothing, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, entered each failed motion in the minutes.
exclusions.C: The delay ran on into winter while the council waited for a majority.
exclusions.D: The council met eleven times that spring.
exclusions.E: The minutes for the following week record the cost of clearing the site, which came to £41.

WV7-P01.5.note: The narration sets a £300 repair against eleven fruitless meetings and ends on the clearing cost, an understated indictment of the council's delay; 'detached' is defensible from the flat, evaluative-word-free reporting, though there is no declared observer narrator.

exclusions.A: It was still sold at four pennies, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had.
exclusions.B: From then on the rye loaf went into the oven on Friday nights alone, and on Saturdays the line for it ran out of the shop and across the square.
exclusions.D: By the first snows of winter the Saturday sales would regularly break ten dozen.
exclusions.E: The Grey Hen's three dozen now had to be bought from the back of a queue that formed at dawn, and Hob spent his Saturday mornings stamping in the cold behind his own customers, while his cook asked daily how the clever idea was getting on.

WV7-P02.4.note: Sales that 'break ten dozen' go past that figure, consistent with the queue running across the square, so the sense is exceed.

exclusions.A: Ada took the plan gladly, since it kept the loaf exactly as Nell had made it.
exclusions.B: It was still sold at four pennies, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had.
exclusions.C: From then on the rye loaf went into the oven on Friday nights alone, and on Saturdays the line for it ran out of the shop and across the square.
exclusions.D: By the first snows of winter the Saturday sales would regularly break ten dozen.

WV7-P02.5.note: The narrator shows Ada's choice keeping Nell's promise and succeeding (unchanged loaf and price, long queues, record sales), an approving view; 'amused' is defensible because the closing irony about Hob colours the plan, though that humour is aimed at Hob rather than at Ada's decision.
